objective: By the end of this lesson you can turn a true course into a compass heading with the wind triangle, variation and deviation, plan and keep a flight log, and fly a leg by pilotage and dead reckoning within commercial tolerances: within 2 NM of the route, within 3 minutes of each checkpoint ETA, altitude within 100 feet and heading within 10 degrees.
why: Pilotage and dead reckoning still work when the screens go dark, and the FAA says every good pilot thinks about a flight in terms of the wind triangle [[1:401|PHAK 16-14]]. The commercial checkride uses the same task as the private one, but every skill tolerance is tighter (ACS CA.VI.A.S5 to S7), so loose habits that passed before will not pass now.

warmup: Think first: on your private checkride you could be 3 NM off course and 5 minutes late at a checkpoint and still pass. On the commercial checkride the limits are 2 NM and 3 minutes. At 150 knots, how many nautical miles is 3 minutes? And if your heading drifts 10 degrees and nobody notices, how long until you are 2 NM off the line?

chunks.title: Pilotage and dead reckoning at the commercial standard

body.p: Pilotage means finding your way by looking at landmarks and checkpoints. It works on any route that has enough good checkpoints, and it is usually flown together with dead reckoning [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

Dead reckoning works it out with numbers: time, airspeed, distance and direction, corrected for wind, give you a heading and a groundspeed. The heading keeps you on the line, and the groundspeed tells you when you should reach each checkpoint and the destination [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

The two methods check each other. Except over water, dead reckoning is normally used with pilotage, and the computed heading and groundspeed are constantly watched and corrected by what you see at each checkpoint [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]. Pilotage tells you where you are. Dead reckoning tells you where you should be and when.

Private (ACS PA.VI.A)
Commercial (ACS CA.VI.A)

body.p: The knowledge and risk elements are word for word the same in both ACS documents. Only the skill tolerances change. Both also ask you to give a destination estimate (ACS CA.VI.A.S6).

callout.text: Application: put the tolerances into distance. At 150 knots, 3 minutes is 7.5 NM of flying. A steady 10 degree heading error puts you 2 NM off the line after about 11.5 NM. So the heading tolerance alone will not keep you inside the position tolerance; you have to check position at every checkpoint.

check.q: Which two commercial skill tolerances are measured at checkpoints rather than all the time?
check.a: Position within 2 NM of the planned route and arrival within 3 minutes of the initial or revised ETA (ACS CA.VI.A.S5, S6).

chunks.title: From true course to compass heading

body.p: You measure the course on the chart from true north, but you steer by a compass that points toward magnetic north and is pulled around by the airplane itself. Three things stand between the chart line and the number you fly: variation, deviation and wind correction [[1:394|PHAK 16-7]].

Draw the line from the center of the departure airport to the center of the destination, and measure its direction with a plotter at a meridian near the middle of the line. That is the true course [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]] [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]. Then follow one fixed sequence: TC plus or minus WCA gives true heading, plus or minus variation gives magnetic heading, plus or minus deviation gives compass heading [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].

bullets: WCA: add if the wind is from the right of the course, subtract if from the left [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]].

Variation: add west, subtract east, 'east is least and west is best' [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Take it from the nearest isogonic line, and if it changes along the route, apply it along the route [[1:394|PHAK 16-7]].
Deviation: read it from the card near the compass, usually given every 30 degrees; interpolate in your head for headings in between [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

body.p: Reading the card: it says what to steer for each magnetic heading. For 060 you steer 057, for west (270) you steer 274 [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. The PHAK's own example: if the correction is 0 at 180 and +2 at 210, use +1 at 195 [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

Deviation is not fixed forever. The magnetic fields inside the airplane change with landing shocks, vibration, maintenance and new equipment, so the compass should be checked now and then by 'swinging' it on a compass rose [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Only AMTs can adjust the compass or fill out the correction card. Pilots must also notice equipment that can upset it, such as radios, pitot heat or magnetic cargo [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]].

callout.text: True Virgins Make Dull Company: TC plus or minus WCA = TH, plus or minus Variation = MH, plus or minus Deviation = CH. (The order is from [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]]; the phrase is only a memory aid.)

Winds aloft forecasts are given relative to true north [[1:323|PHAK 13-13]]. Put them into the wind triangle against the true course. Mixing a magnetic course with a true wind puts the whole variation into your WCA as an error.

check.q: Your magnetic heading is 225. Using Figure 16-12, what compass heading do you steer?
check.a: The card shows 212 for 210 and 243 for 240, corrections of +2 and +3. Halfway between, about +2.5, so steer about 227 to 228 [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

chunks.title: The wind triangle, by drawing and by trig

body.p: An airplane moves in two ways at once: through the air at its airspeed, and along with the air mass as it moves over the ground. After an hour it is where those two motions put it [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]] [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. A pilot in a 70-knot gale would feel nothing unless he looked at the ground [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]].

The wind triangle is the basis of dead reckoning [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]. The PHAK draws it in four steps: mark the departure point E and the true course; draw the wind line from E downwind, as long as the wind speed; then lay a ruler from the end of the wind line (W) so that the true airspeed length meets the course line at P. E to P is the groundspeed, and the angle at P is the WCA [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]].
The PHAK example: TC 090, wind from 045 at 40 knots, TAS 120. The answer is a WCA of 14 degrees left (TH 076) and a groundspeed of 88 knots [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]].

Application: an E6B or electronic computer solves the same triangle [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]], and you can check it with two lines of trig. Wind angle = wind direction minus true course. Crosswind = wind speed x sin(wind angle). Headwind = wind speed x cos(wind angle). WCA = arcsin(crosswind / TAS). GS = TAS x cos(WCA) minus headwind. For the PHAK example: wind angle 45 degrees, crosswind 28.3, headwind 28.3, WCA = arcsin(28.3/120) = 13.6 degrees, GS = 120 x 0.972 minus 28.3 = 88.3 knots. That matches the 14 degrees and 88 knots in the book.

callout.text: A common drawing error is pointing the wind arrow toward the direction the wind comes from. Draw it downwind, in the direction the air is moving [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]].

check.q: With the wind from the left of the course, does the WCA make the true heading larger or smaller than the true course?
check.a: Smaller. A wind from the left is corrected by pointing the nose to the left, so the WCA is subtracted [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]] [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]].

body.p: Three formulas do all the work: time = distance / GS, distance = GS x time, and GS = distance / time. Convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60 [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. A knot is one nautical mile per hour; to turn knots into mph, multiply by 1.15 [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]].

Fuel follows time, and time follows groundspeed. Fuel burn per hour stays about the same at a given TAS, so when there is wind you must use the groundspeed to work out fuel [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Plan for start and taxi, the higher burn in the climb (where your groundspeed is also lower), the cruise, and a reserve [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

chunks.title: True airspeed, density altitude and power setting

body.p: The airspeed indicator does not show the speed you plan with. TAS is calibrated airspeed corrected for altitude and nonstandard temperature. For the same CAS, TAS goes up as you climb. The most accurate way to find it is a flight computer with CAS, pressure altitude and temperature; the rule of thumb is to add 2 percent to CAS for each 1,000 ft [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. It is the standard-atmosphere altitude that matches the real air density, and the higher it is, the lower the airplane's performance [[1:259|PHAK 11-3]] [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]]. Application: hot air means a higher density altitude, thinner air and a higher TAS for the same indicated speed.

Power setting selection comes from the POH cruise tables. A cruise power setting table gives the power setting plus the fuel flow and TAS at that altitude [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. In the sample table (65 percent power, 2,800 lb) read across: at 6,000 ft on a standard day it is 2,450 RPM, 20.4 in Hg, 11.5 GPH and 158 knots [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].

bullets: Altitude helps TAS at the same power: standard day, 150 knots at sea level and 163 knots at 10,000 ft for the same 11.5 GPH [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].
Heat helps TAS at the same percent power: at 6,000 ft, 155 knots at ISA minus 20, 158 at standard, 161 at ISA plus 20 [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].
In the shaded rows the engine is at full throttle (note 2): fuel flow starts to drop, and higher up the TAS drops too [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].
Another sample chart notes that maximum cruise is normally limited to 75 percent power [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]].
Between rows, interpolate. At 7,000 ft standard day, halfway between 158 and 161 knots is about 159.5 knots (application of [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]]).

body.p: Mixture is part of the power setting. As you climb, the mixture gets richer, which can foul the plugs and cost power; leaning reduces fuel flow to match the thinner air. Use the POH leaning procedure, often with an EGT gauge [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

check.q: Using Figure 11-28, what TAS and fuel flow do you plan at 10,000 ft on a standard day?
check.a: 163 knots and 11.5 GPH at 2,450 RPM and 19.9 in Hg [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].

body.p: The magnetic compass is a required instrument for powered aircraft under VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(3)]]. Its float rides on a pivot and can tilt only to about 18 degrees of bank; steeper than that, its readings are erratic [[1:225|PHAK 8-23]]. It is simple, but it has several errors [[1:226|PHAK 8-24]].

head: Error
What happens
What you do
rows: True and magnetic north differ; same on every heading at one place [[1:226|PHAK 8-24]]
Fields inside the airplane; changes with heading, not with location [[1:226|PHAK 8-24]]
In a bank, dip tilts the card, so it shows the wrong heading during the turn; worse near the poles [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Stop the turn before the heading [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
The same dip error, the other way: the card runs ahead of the real turn [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Let it pass the heading before you stop [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
On east or west headings, speeding up shows a turn to the north, slowing shows a turn to the south (ANDS) [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Read it only in steady, unaccelerated flight
All the errors together swing the card [[1:229|PHAK 8-27]]
Use the average of the swings when setting the heading indicator [[1:229|PHAK 8-27]]

body.p: Why turning errors exist: the float's center of gravity hangs below the pivot so the card stays level. Once the airplane banks, the vertical pull of the earth's field (dip) tilts the card and drags it around [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. Close to the magnetic poles the horizontal pull is too weak and the compass is unusable [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

The rule of thumb in the PHAK for how far to lead or lag: 15 degrees plus half the latitude. Near 40 degrees north, stop a turn to north 35 degrees before the heading; near 30 degrees, let a turn to south go 30 degrees past it [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

callout.text: UNOS: Undershoot North, Overshoot South. ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South. (UNOS is a common teaching phrase; ANDS is the PHAK's own [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].)

check.q: You speed up on a heading of 270. Which way does the compass swing, and is the airplane turning?
check.a: It shows a turn toward north. The airplane is not turning; it is acceleration error, which appears on east and west headings [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

chunks.title: Turns to headings with only the compass

body.p: In most small airplanes the magnetic compass is the only direction instrument that does not depend on other instruments or a power source [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. If the heading indicator fails or precesses, you still have to hold your heading within 10 degrees (ACS CA.VI.A.S7).

bullets: On a north heading, a turn to the east or west at first shows a turn the opposite way (the compass lags) [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
On a south heading, a turn toward east or west shows more turn than is really happening (the compass leads) [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
On an east or west heading, it reads correctly when the turn starts [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
Holding north or south, climbing, diving or changing speed causes no error [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

body.p: The IFH method: with 15 to 18 degrees of bank, the lead or lag is about equal to your latitude. At 30 degrees latitude, turning from east to north, start the roll-out at 037 (30 plus half of a 15 degree bank). Turning from east to south, start at 203. From the west: 323 for north and 157 for south [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Turning to east or west from a northerly heading, start rolling out 10 to 12 degrees early; from a southerly heading, about 5 degrees early [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

Timed turns are the backup to the backup. A standard-rate turn is 3 degrees per second, so 45 degrees takes 15 seconds; a half-standard-rate turn takes 30 seconds for the same 45 degrees. Start timing as the second hand passes a cardinal point and begin the roll-out when the time is up [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

callout.text: Before the checkride, practice: cover the heading indicator, turn to assigned headings using the compass, and check the result against the uncovered gyro. Use small banks and smooth roll-outs, then wait for the card to settle; abrupt attitude or airspeed changes make it swing [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

check.q: At 30 degrees latitude you are heading west and must turn right to north with a 15 degree bank. Using the IFH method, where do you start the roll-out?

chunks.title: Reading the land: topography and obstacles

body.p: The sectional is drawn at 1:500,000, large enough to fly by sight [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p.10]]. On it, 1 inch is 6.86 NM, about 8 SM [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]]. The FAA shows the shape of the land in five ways: contour lines, shaded relief, color tints, obstruction symbols and Maximum Elevation Figures [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p.10]].

bullets: Contours: basic lines every 500 ft, intermediate lines often every 250 ft. Close lines mean steep ground [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p.10]].
Shaded relief: drawn as if the light came from the northwest, because that is how our eyes expect to see it [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p.10]].
Color tints: from light green for low ground to dark brown for high ground [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].

Obstacles: man-made objects more than 200 ft AGL are usually shown (more than 299 ft AGL in the yellow city tint). In crowded areas only the highest is shown, with a group symbol [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].
UC beside an obstacle means under construction or reported but not verified [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].
Wind turbine obstruction lights sit on the hub, which can be 200 to 300 ft below the unlighted blade tips [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].
MEF: the highest terrain or obstacle in a quadrant, rounded up to the next 100 ft [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p.12]].

body.p: Charts are not perfect. Charts are generally flight-checked every four years [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]], new roads and structures may not appear until the next edition, and antennas held up by almost invisible guy wires can be hard to see [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. TV transmitting towers can stand more than 1,500 ft above the terrain [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]].

callout.text: Never approach an area of antennas less than 500 ft above the tallest one [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Use current charts. Sectionals are updated every 56 days [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]].

check.q: A wind turbine farm is marked with its highest turbine. Why is its obstruction light a poor guide to the real top?
check.a: The light is on the hub, which can be 200 to 300 ft below the rotating blade tips, and the blades are not lighted [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].

chunks.title: Choosing the route, altitude and checkpoints

body.p: Route: check the weather first to see whether the flight is possible and which route is best [[1:404|PHAK 16-17]]. A direct line is simplest, but a route via a VOR that makes navigating easier is fine [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]]. Check the airspace on and beside the route, and find the highest terrain and the tallest obstruction [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]]. Look for airports or landing areas along the way and aids you could use in a diversion [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

Altitude: above 3,000 ft AGL, a VFR cruising altitude must fit the magnetic course: odd thousands plus 500 on 000 to 179, even thousands plus 500 on 180 to 359 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]] [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]. Stay above the minimum safe altitudes, including enough height for an emergency landing anywhere [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]. Then weigh winds, power and fuel, and visibility: AC 90-48E recommends flying above a haze layer [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]]. In the PHAK example, 5,500 ft is picked to fly over the Class C and D airspace and clear all obstructions [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].

Checkpoints: pick prominent features that other features help confirm, such as roads, rivers, railroads, lakes and power lines [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Good choices are large towns, large lakes and rivers, or combinations such as a town with an airport, highways and a railroad. Normally pick towns shown as yellow splashes, not small circles, which may be only a few houses [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]].

bullets: Brackets: features on both sides of the course, such as highways, rivers or mountains, keep you from drifting far off course [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Never rely on a single checkpoint. Pick plenty, so if you miss one you look for the next while holding the heading [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Charted VFR checkpoints are marked with a small flag; the underlined name is the checkpoint's proper name [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p.33]].
At night, rotating beacons, lighted obstructions, towns and highway traffic make good checkpoints; draw the course line in black so it shows in low light [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

callout.text: Application for the 2 NM standard: on a sectional, 2 NM is only about 0.3 inch (2 / 6.86). A checkpoint a quarter inch off the line is 1.7 NM away [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Choose checkpoints on or very near the line, or ones you can measure from.

check.q: Your magnetic course is 198 and you will cruise more than 3,000 ft AGL below 18,000 ft MSL. Is 7,500 ft correct?
check.a: No. A magnetic course of 180 to 359 needs an even thousand plus 500, such as 6,500 or 8,500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]].

chunks.title: The flight log: build it, then fly it

body.p: The flight log is where pilotage and dead reckoning meet. The PHAK's sample log has, for each leg: course, altitude, wind, WCA, true heading, variation, magnetic heading, deviation, compass heading, distance, groundspeed, time and fuel, and then for each checkpoint the estimated and actual time and groundspeed [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].

body.p: Table: built from the sample log [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]] and the PHAK's instruction to note headings and times as the trip progresses and adjust heading, GS and time [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

On the checkride you fly with pre-computed headings, groundspeeds and times and check them against landmarks (ACS CA.VI.A.S3). The 3 minute tolerance is measured against the initial or revised ETA, and you must give a destination estimate (ACS CA.VI.A.S6). So the revised ETA is part of the job: after each checkpoint, work out the actual groundspeed and push the new times forward.

callout.text: Do the arithmetic before engine start for every line you can. In flight, the PHAK says to use every shortcut and rule of thumb, because your attention is split between flying, figuring and scanning [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

check.q: You pass checkpoint A at 1012 and checkpoint B, 26 NM later, at 1025. The destination is 54 NM past B. What is your destination estimate?

body.p: A plan is a forecast. The forecast wind is the weak link, so expect your real groundspeed and drift to be different. You can measure groundspeed in flight by timing a known distance [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]], and the PHAK says to keep watching the computed heading and groundspeed and correct them by pilotage at each checkpoint [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

bullets: Late or early at a checkpoint: work out the actual groundspeed and use it for the rest of the leg. Then compare fuel: a lower groundspeed means more fuel for the same distance [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Off to one side: the track is drifting, so your WCA is wrong. A wind from the left drifts you right; correct by heading farther left [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]].
If confused, hold the heading. A turn away from it is how pilots get lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

If the destination no longer works: divert. Note the time on course, use the nearest winds aloft to work out a new heading and GS, then a new arrival time and fuel. In an emergency, turn first and figure later [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

body.p: The sources do not give a formula for how much to correct the heading after drifting off course. Application: if you are 2 NM right of the line after 20 NM, the track is about 6 degrees right of course (arctan of 2/20 = 5.7), so you need roughly that much more left correction just to stop the drift, plus a bit more to get back to the line. Recheck at the next checkpoint.

callout.text: The commercial standard is 2 NM and 3 minutes (ACS CA.VI.A.S5, S6). Small errors that you ignore for two checkpoints will usually be too big by the third. Correct early, in small amounts.

check.q: Your planned groundspeed was 124 knots. Two checkpoints 21 NM apart take 12 minutes, and 63 NM remain. What is your new time to go?

chunks.title: Risk: traffic, distraction and getting lost

body.p: Pilotage pulls your eyes to the chart, the log and the ground, which is exactly when you are not looking for traffic. Every pilot, IFR or VFR, must keep watching so as to see and avoid other aircraft when weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

bullets: Scan in short, regular eye movements of no more than 10 degrees, looking at each area for at least 1 second [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]].

The eye can only focus on and recognize things in a narrow area of about 10 to 15 degrees, and with nothing to focus on (above haze, no horizon) it tends not to focus at all [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.7]] [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.5]].
In level cruise, make gentle banks left and right to see past the nose and wings. High wings block the view above, low wings below [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Flying into the sun, glare can hide an airplane that would stand out with the sun behind you [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.10]].
Be extra watchful near VORs and VFR waypoints, where GPS accuracy puts many airplanes on the same line; turn on the landing light there [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

body.p: Distraction and lost situational awareness: fixation means locking attention on one task and forgetting what is going on around you [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]. In flight, give priority to flying the airplane while you split attention between navigation and planning [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]]. Load VFR waypoints on the ground; avoid programming routes once airborne [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

If you do get lost: climb, if traffic and weather allow, for better radio and radar coverage; read a town name on a water tower; use VOR bearings or GPS; and call any facility on the chart. ATC may give vectors or direction-finding help. If it turns serious, use 121.5 MHz and squawk 7700 [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

callout.text: Heads-down habit: look at the chart in short pieces, then scan, then look again. Fold the chart to the leg before takeoff so you are not wrestling paper over a checkpoint.

check.q: Another airplane converging from your right at about your altitude stays in the same spot on your windshield. Who has the right-of-way, and what does the steady position tell you?
check.a: The airplane on the right has the right-of-way [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. An airplane that seems motionless is likely on a collision course and can suddenly 'bloom' into view [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]]. Give way now.

chunks.title: Risk: unplanned fuel and power use

body.p: Fuel burn depends on engine condition, propeller pitch, RPM, mixture and the percent of power used [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Several things can make the real fuel use higher than the plan: a stronger headwind, which adds time [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]; a power setting above the plan; or a mixture not leaned at altitude [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

bullets: Know your airplane's burn from the cruise charts or from experience [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]], and keep a record of past burns to support the planning numbers [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]].
At each checkpoint compare fuel used with fuel planned. A slower groundspeed means more hours, and fuel goes by hours [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Remember the legal floor: 30 minutes of fuel at normal cruise after the first landing point by day, 45 at night [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]].
If the numbers get close, land early for fuel. The PHAK rule: be on the surface before your planned fuel time runs out or the gauge shows low [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

body.p: Power and altitude change fuel too. In the sample table at 65 percent power the fuel flow is 11.5 GPH up to 10,000 ft, then falls to 9.4 GPH at 16,000 ft on a standard day as the engine runs out of throttle [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]]. A different altitude changes the TAS, and a different power setting changes both TAS and fuel flow, so rework both.

callout.text: Fuel gauges and fuel totalizers can both be wrong. Fly the clock as well as the gauge, and act on the more pessimistic number.

check.q: You planned 11.5 GPH but the fuel flow shows 13 GPH at the same RPM. What is the first thing to check?
check.a: The mixture. A mixture that was not leaned for altitude burns extra fuel; lean per the POH [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. Then rework the fuel remaining and reserve [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Wind drawn toward the direction it comes from
Magnetic course used with a true wind
Winds aloft are true; work the triangle on the true course [[1:323|PHAK 13-13]]
West is best (add), east is least (subtract) [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]
Use groundspeed when there is wind [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]
Use yellow city tints and features that confirm each other [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]]
Turning to search for a missed checkpoint
Hold the heading and look for the next one [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]
Reading the compass in a turn or while changing speed
Read it straight, level and steady [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Altitude creeps while reading the chart
Trim, then check the altimeter every scan; the limit is 100 ft (ACS CA.VI.A.S7)
Revise after each checkpoint; the 3 minutes is against the revised ETA (ACS CA.VI.A.S6)

callout.text: Say it out loud for the examiner at each checkpoint: 'Over the town at 14:22, two minutes late, groundspeed 128, new ETA 14:51, fuel on plan, holding 066.' That one sentence shows S1, S3, S5 and S6 at once.

check.q: The examiner asks for your destination estimate halfway through the leg. What do you base it on?
check.a: The actual groundspeed between your last checkpoints and the distance remaining, not the planned groundspeed [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]] (ACS CA.VI.A.S6).

chunks.title: Reading the chart: obstacles and mountain terrain

body.p: Pilotage gets harder as the land gets rougher. In the mountains, contour lines, spot elevations and the MEF tell you what is ahead. On the excerpt, the blue 13 with a small 5 is 13,500 ft MSL, so any leg in that quadrant needs a margin above that figure, not just above the last peak you saw [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p 13]].

Spot elevations also help you match the chart to the ground. Red River airport shows 8617, and the spot elevations around it (12584, 12441, 12734) tell you which peak is which. A mountain pass symbol is not a recommended route, and the elevation printed for a pass is not a recommended clearance altitude [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p 13]].

Now the obstacles. Every obstacle symbol shows its top in MSL (italic) and its height above ground in parentheses. A group symbol means several obstacles close together. A wind turbine farm is an outlined area with the top of the highest turbine, and UC after the number means that turbine is unverified, so allow extra room [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p 33]].

Use these as checkpoints too, but only after you read the height: a tower group 1,432 ft above ground is a hazard on your track, not just a landmark. Keep your position within 2 NM of the planned route so the obstacles you planned around stay where you expect them (ACS CA.VI.A.S5).

check.q: A group obstruction symbol reads 4977 over (1432). Which number do you use to see if you clear it at 5,500 ft MSL?
check.a: The 4977. It is the top in MSL, so 5,500 ft clears it by 523 ft. The 1432 is height above ground, which only matters if you are measuring from the terrain [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p 33]].

scenario.title: The checkride leg that ran slow
scenario.setup: Commercial checkride. You planned the first leg of your cross-country: true course 074, 131 NM, variation 4 degrees W, cruise at 7,500 ft in an airplane whose POH cruise table matches Figure 11-28. The forecast wind at 7,500 is 330 at 26 knots (true). You planned 65 percent power. Your first checkpoint is a town with a highway and railroad 24 NM after level-off. At the second checkpoint, 28 NM farther, you find you took 12 minutes. There is haze, and the examiner is chatting with you about your career.

questions.q: Is 7,500 ft a legal VFR cruising altitude for this course, and what TAS and fuel flow do you plan there?
questions.a: Magnetic course is 074 + 4 = 078, so odd thousands plus 500 apply and 7,500 is correct [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]]. Standard day, interpolating between 158 knots at 6,000 and 161 at 8,000 gives about 160 knots, at 11.5 GPH [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].

questions.q: Work the wind triangle. What WCA, true heading and groundspeed do you plan?
questions.a: Wind angle 330 minus 074 is 256 degrees, which is the same as 104 degrees from the left. Crosswind 26 x sin 104 = 25.2 knots from the left, plus a 6.3-knot tailwind. WCA = arcsin(25.2 / 160) = 9 degrees left, TH 065, GS = 160 x cos 9 + 6.3 = 164 knots. Apply the WCA with the PHAK sign rule [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]].

questions.q: What compass heading goes on the log?
questions.a: TH 065 plus 4 W = MH 069 (west is added) [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Figure 16-12 gives -3 at 060 and -4 at 090, so about -3 at 069. CH about 066 [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

questions.q: 28 NM in 12 minutes: what is your actual groundspeed, and what do you owe the examiner now?
questions.a: 28 / 12 x 60 = 140 knots, not 164 [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. Revise the ETAs for the next checkpoints and give a new destination estimate; the 3 minute limit is measured against the revised ETA (ACS CA.VI.A.S6). The PHAK says to adjust heading, GS and time as the trip progresses [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

questions.q: The groundspeed drop also changes fuel. What do you check?
questions.a: Fuel goes by time, and time by groundspeed [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. If the whole 131 NM leg ran at 140 knots it would take about 56 minutes instead of 48, about 10.8 gallons instead of 9.2 at 11.5 GPH. Check that you still land with at least the legal reserve [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]] and your own margin.

questions.q: Haze, a talking examiner and a recalculation all at once. How do you manage the risk?
questions.a: Fly the airplane first and split attention between navigation and planning [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]]. Keep the scan going in short movements [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]]; haze makes traffic hard to see [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]]. It is fine to tell the examiner you need a minute to navigate.

skills.do: Prepare a complete flight log before the flight and keep it up to date in flight: times over checkpoints, actual groundspeed, revised ETAs and fuel.
skills.practice: Plan the PHAK Chickasha to Guthrie trip and compare your log to Figure 16-26 [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]]; then fill in the actual columns on every training cross-country [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

skills.do: Find and confirm your position from landmarks, matching the chart to the ground.
skills.practice: Pick checkpoints that other features confirm and bracket the course with highways or rivers [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]; fly legs with the GPS covered.

skills.do: Fly pre-computed compass headings, groundspeeds and times, and check them against landmarks at each checkpoint.
skills.practice: Work every leg with the wind triangle and the TC to CH sequence before flight [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]] [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]], then fly the computed heading and see how well it holds.

skills.do: Use the magnetic compass to navigate and to turn to headings, allowing for its errors.
skills.practice: With the heading indicator covered, turn to headings using the IFH lead and lag points and timed turns [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

skills.do: Show the examiner your position is within 2 NM of the planned route.
skills.practice: At each checkpoint, estimate your distance from the course line using the chart scale (1 inch = 6.86 NM) and correct the heading early [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

skills.do: Arrive at each en route checkpoint within 3 minutes of the initial or revised ETA, and give a destination estimate.
skills.practice: After each checkpoint, compute actual GS and new ETAs out loud [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]; aim to be inside 1 minute in training.

skills.do: Hold the selected altitude within 100 ft and heading within 10 degrees while you navigate.
skills.practice: Trim carefully and practice chart work in short looks while a CFI calls out every 50 ft and 5 degree drift [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]].

quiz.q: On a sectional, what do the broken magenta lines marked with degrees east or west show?
options: Contour lines of equal terrain elevation, labeled in feet above sea level
Isogonic lines, used to convert between true and magnetic direction
Lines of equal compass deviation for your airplane, used to correct the compass
The boundaries of each MEF quadrant, with the clearance altitude printed in each
quiz.why: Isogonic lines are broken magenta lines joining points of equal magnetic variation; the line of zero variation is the agonic line [[1:393|PHAK 16-6]]. Deviation is not charted; it comes from the card in your own airplane [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

quiz.q: Dead reckoning by itself produces which two results?
options: True airspeed and density altitude
Position and altitude
Variation and deviation
Heading and groundspeed
quiz.why: Dead reckoning uses time, airspeed, distance and direction; the products, adjusted for wind, are heading and groundspeed [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

quiz.q: Who may adjust the magnetic compass and fill out its correction card?
options: Only an AMT
Any certificated pilot
The pilot in command, after a flight test
Only the airplane manufacturer
quiz.why: Only AMTs can adjust the compass or complete the compass correction card; pilots fly compass headings using the card [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]].

quiz.q: TC 165, TAS 110 knots, forecast wind 210 at 18. About what true heading do you fly?
quiz.why: Wind is 45 degrees from the right. Crosswind 18 x sin 45 = 12.7; WCA = arcsin(12.7/110) = 6.6, about 7 degrees right, added because the wind is from the right [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]. 165 + 7 = 172.

quiz.q: Why should a pilot have the compass deviation checked from time to time?
options: The compass fluid evaporates each year
Variation changes every flight
Landing shocks, vibration, maintenance and new equipment change the airplane's magnetic fields
Deviation changes with the airplane's location
quiz.why: The magnetic forces inside the airplane change because of landing shocks, vibration, mechanical work or changes in equipment, so deviation should be checked occasionally [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Deviation does not depend on location [[1:226|PHAK 8-24]].

quiz.q: Using Figure 11-28, which change raises TAS at the same 65 percent power at 6,000 ft?
options: None; TAS is fixed by percent power
A colder day (ISA minus 20)
Descending to sea level
A hotter day (ISA plus 20)
quiz.why: At 6,000 ft the table shows 155 knots at ISA minus 20, 158 at standard and 161 at ISA plus 20 [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].

quiz.q: Using the IFH method at 30 degrees latitude with a 15 degree bank, where do you start the roll-out when turning from an easterly heading to south?
quiz.why: Keep turning until the compass passes south by the latitude minus half the bank: 180 + 30 minus 7.5, about 203 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. 157 is the point for a turn to south from the west.

quiz.q: How often are VFR sectional and terminal area charts updated, per the Chart Users' Guide?
options: Once a year
Every 28 days
Every 6 months
Every 56 days
quiz.why: Sectionals and TACs are updated every 56 days [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]]. PHAK 16-2 says these charts are revised semiannually [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]]; this lesson follows the current Chart Users' Guide.

quiz.q: In the PHAK Chickasha to Guthrie example, 53 NM at a groundspeed of 106 knots is 30 minutes. Why does the log plan 35 minutes?
options: The wind correction adds 5 minutes
5 minutes are the legal VFR reserve
5 minutes are added for the climb
5 minutes are added for taxi
quiz.why: The total time is 30 minutes plus 5 minutes for climb, 35 minutes, with 4.7 gallons burned at 8 GPH [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]]. The day VFR reserve is 30 minutes, not 5 [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: How far apart are the eye movements in an effective traffic scan, per AC 90-48E?
options: No more than 2 degrees, 5 seconds each
About 30 degrees, half a second each
One sweep of the whole windshield every 10 seconds
No more than 10 degrees, at least 1 second each
quiz.why: Each movement should not exceed 10 degrees, and each area should be looked at for at least 1 second [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]].

quiz.q: A wind turbine farm shows 2894 UC. What does UC mean here?
options: The farm is under control of the nearby tower
The highest turbine's height is unverified
The farm is closed to flight below 1,000 ft
The turbines are lit with red lights at night
quiz.why: The legend says UC is shown after the MSL value when the highest wind turbine is unverified [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p 33]].

quiz.q: A group obstruction symbol reads 4977 over (1432). What does the number in parentheses give?
options: The group's top in ft MSL
The height above ground in ft AGL
The number of obstacles in the group
The distance to the group in feet
quiz.why: The italic number is the top in MSL, and the number in parentheses is the height in feet AGL [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p 33]].

quiz.q: A wind turbine is shown as 2735 over (415). What are the two numbers?
options: Elevation of the base 2,735 ft, 415 turbines
Distance 2,735 ft, height 415 ft
Top 2,735 ft AGL, 415 ft MSL
Top 2,735 ft MSL, 415 ft AGL
quiz.why: Obstacles show the top in MSL and the height in AGL in parentheses [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p 33]].

quiz.q: What is the elevation printed for Red River airport (N02) on the excerpt?
quiz.why: The airport label reads RED RIVER (N02) 8617 122.8, so the elevation is 8,617 ft. 9854 belongs to Red River Pass [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p 13]].

quiz.q: What maximum elevation figure does the quadrant on the excerpt show?
options: 13,500 ft MSL
1,350 ft MSL
13,050 ft MSL
13,161 ft MSL
quiz.why: The blue 13 with a small 5 is 13,500 ft MSL. 13,161 is the circled spot elevation it was built from [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p 13]].

quiz.q: It is a night cross-country in an airplane. Your ETE to the first point of intended landing is 2 hours 10 minutes. What is the minimum fuel endurance to start the flight?
options: 2 hours 10 minutes
2 hours 40 minutes
3 hours 10 minutes
2 hours 55 minutes
quiz.why: At night you need enough fuel to reach the first landing point and then fly at least 45 more minutes at normal cruise: 2:10 + 0:45 = 2:55 [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: TC 315, TAS 150, wind 020 at 28 (true), variation 5 W. Figure 16-12 shows 332 for 330. What compass heading do you steer?
final_quiz.why: Wind 65 degrees from the right: crosswind 25.4, WCA = arcsin(25.4/150) = 9.7, about 10 right, TH 325 [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]. Add 5 W: MH 330 [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Card +2: CH 332 [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. 322 subtracts variation, 328 subtracts deviation, 312 subtracts the WCA.

final_quiz.q: Same leg: TC 315, TAS 150, wind 020 at 28. What groundspeed do you plan?
options: About 136 knots
About 122 knots
About 150 knots
About 162 knots
final_quiz.why: Headwind component 28 x cos 65 = 11.8. GS = 150 x cos 9.7 minus 11.8 = 147.9 minus 11.8 = about 136 knots (application of the wind triangle [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]]).

final_quiz.q: On the commercial checkride you are 2.5 NM right of course at a checkpoint, on time, on altitude and heading. What is true?
options: You pass because time, altitude and heading are good
You are outside the 2 NM position tolerance and need to correct
You are inside the tolerance, which is 3 NM
Position only matters at the destination
final_quiz.why: Commercial applicants must verify position within 2 NM of the planned route (ACS CA.VI.A.S5); the 3 NM figure is the private standard (ACS PA.VI.A.S5). Pilotage depends on ample checkpoints so you do not drift far off course [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

final_quiz.q: On a sectional, about how far from the course line is the edge of the commercial 2 NM position tolerance?
options: About 0.3 inch
About 0.5 inch
About 0.1 inch
About 0.7 inch
final_quiz.why: 1 inch = 6.86 NM on a sectional [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]], so 2 NM is 2 / 6.86 = 0.29, about 0.3 inch (ACS CA.VI.A.S5). Half an inch is 3.43 NM, outside the tolerance [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

final_quiz.q: You planned 8,000 ft on a standard day with Figure 11-28 (161 knots). Clouds force you down to 6,000 ft at the same 65 percent power. What do you now plan?
options: 161 knots at 11.5 GPH
158 knots at 11.5 GPH
158 knots at 10.9 GPH
155 knots at 11.5 GPH
final_quiz.why: Standard day at 6,000 ft: 2,450 RPM, 20.4 in Hg, 11.5 GPH, 158 knots [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]]. 155 knots is the ISA minus 20 column. Rework your times with the lower groundspeed.

final_quiz.q: Your winds aloft forecast says 270 at 30. Your magnetic course is 255 and variation is 12 E. What do you put in the wind triangle?
options: True course 243 with the wind 258 at 30
Magnetic course 255 with the wind 270 at 30
True course 267 with the wind 270 at 30
Magnetic course 255 with the wind 282 at 30
final_quiz.why: Winds aloft are given relative to true north [[1:323|PHAK 13-13]], and the triangle starts from the true course [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]. East variation is subtracted going from true to magnetic [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]], so going back you add it: TC = 255 + 12 = 267.

final_quiz.q: You need to turn from north to east using only the magnetic compass. When does the IFH say to start rolling out?
options: About 5 degrees before the compass reads east
About 10 to 12 degrees before the compass reads east
When the compass reads exactly east
About 30 degrees past east on the compass
final_quiz.why: Turning to east or west from a northerly heading, start the roll-out about 10 to 12 degrees before; from a southerly heading, about 5 degrees before [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

final_quiz.q: You hold a standard-rate turn to change heading 60 degrees on the clock. How long do you hold it?
options: 15 seconds
30 seconds
20 seconds
40 seconds
final_quiz.why: Standard rate is 3 degrees per second (45 degrees in 15 seconds), so 60 / 3 = 20 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

final_quiz.q: Your 210 NM leg crosses isogonic lines from 2 degrees E near departure to 6 degrees E near the destination. How do you handle variation?
options: Use the departure value for the whole leg
Apply the variation along the route as it changes, so the magnetic heading changes too
Average the two and apply it only at the destination
Ignore it; only deviation matters for the compass heading
final_quiz.why: Use the nearest isogonic line, and where the variation changes along the route, apply the values along the route [[1:394|PHAK 16-7]]. Variation must be converted before deviation, in the TC to CH sequence [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]].

final_quiz.q: You fly 15 NM with a heading 10 degrees off and do not notice. About how far are you from the course line, and does it pass?
options: About 2.6 NM, outside the 2 NM standard
About 1.5 NM, inside the 2 NM standard
About 0.3 NM, inside the 2 NM standard
About 5.2 NM, outside the 2 NM standard
final_quiz.why: Application: 15 x sin 10 = 2.6 NM. The position standard is 2 NM (ACS CA.VI.A.S5), so a heading error inside the 10 degree limit (ACS CA.VI.A.S7) can still fail position if you do not check checkpoints. Checkpoints and brackets keep you from drifting too far off course [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

final_quiz.q: On a night cross-country, which make good visual checkpoints according to the AFH?
options: Rotating beacons, lighted obstructions, and lights of towns and highways
Rivers and small lakes
Contour lines and shaded relief
Unlighted VFR checkpoint flags
final_quiz.why: At night, airport beacons, lighted obstructions, lights of cities or towns, and highway traffic make excellent visual checkpoints [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

final_quiz.q: In the PHAK Chickasha to Guthrie example, why was 5,500 ft chosen?
options: To fly over the Class C and D airspace, clear obstructions, and fit an odd thousand plus 500 for the course
Because the wind was strongest there
Because the flight log says 8,000 ft is too high
Because 5,500 is the MEF for the area
final_quiz.why: The wind was no factor, so 5,500 was chosen to stay above the Class C and D airspace with clearance over all obstructions and to fit the rule for magnetic courses 0 to 179 [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].

final_quiz.q: Over checkpoint 2 you are 4 minutes later than the ETA you revised at checkpoint 1. What does the commercial ACS say?
options: Revised ETAs are not allowed on the checkride, only the initial ETA counts
You are fine because the private tolerance of 5 minutes applies to this checkride
Only the destination time counts, not the time at each checkpoint
You are outside the 3 minute tolerance against the revised ETA
final_quiz.why: Commercial: within 3 minutes of the initial or revised ETA (ACS CA.VI.A.S6). Four minutes is outside it. The 5 minute figure is private (ACS PA.VI.A.S6). As the trip progresses, note headings and time and adjust heading, groundspeed and time [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

final_quiz.q: On the excerpt, which feature is circled in yellow?
options: The Red River Pass label
The Red River airport symbol
The Costilla Lake outline
The 13161 spot elevation
final_quiz.why: The yellow circle surrounds the 13161 spot elevation used to build the MEF [[2:13|Chart Users' Guide p 13]].

final_quiz.q: Which legend row is described as at least two obstacles, 1,000 ft AGL or higher, in the group?
options: The wind turbine labeled 2735 over (415)
The two-spire symbol with 2889 over (1217)
The legend row labeled 1062 over (227)
The dotted outline of the wind farm, 2894 UC
final_quiz.why: The legend lists the two-spire symbol for at least two in the group at 1,000 ft AGL and higher [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p 33]].

final_quiz.q: You fly pilotage over a town. The highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally of your track is 650 ft above the surface. What is the lowest cruise altitude above the surface over the town?
options: 650 ft
final_quiz.why: Over a congested area the minimum is 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within a 2,000 ft horizontal radius, so 650 + 1,000 = 1,650 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

takeaways: Pilotage tells you where you are; dead reckoning tells you where you should be and when.
TC, WCA, TH, variation, MH, deviation, CH: same order every time; winds aloft are true.
Fuel follows time, and time follows groundspeed. Refigure both at every checkpoint.
Compass: stop early turning to north, late turning to south; ANDS on east and west.
Choose confirmable checkpoints near the line; 2 NM is only 0.3 inch on a sectional.
Commercial limits: 2 NM, 3 minutes from the revised ETA, 100 ft, 10 degrees.
Short looks down, long looks out: navigation never replaces the traffic scan.
cfi_notes: PHAK Figure 16-19 illustrates the idea of the wind triangle. Its printed numbers (120 knots, wind 020 at 35, heading 080, a 10 degree drift angle, an 8 degree left correction and 110 knots) do not solve exactly: trig gives a WCA of about 16 degrees and a GS of about 103 knots [[1:401|PHAK 16-14]]. The Figure 16-21 example (14 degrees, 88 knots) does solve [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]], so use it for worked numbers.

PHAK 16-2 says sectionals and TACs are revised semiannually, and 16-17 says a chart may be up to 6 months old [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]] [[1:404|PHAK 16-17]]. The current Chart Users' Guide says these charts are updated every 56 days [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]]. This lesson teaches the 56-day cycle.

The PHAK Chickasha example reads the variation as '6.30 E' and rounds it to 7 E [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]]. Read as 6 degrees 30 minutes, 7 is a fair rounding; read as a decimal 6.3, it would round to 6. Use it to show students to read the isogonic value off the chart themselves.

IFH 5-13 prints the southerly example as '15 + 15 + 30 degrees' after passing the heading [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]; PHAK 8-26 gives the intended 15 + 15 = 30 [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. The IFH 7-22 method (latitude, plus or minus half the bank) gives slightly different numbers [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Both are rules of thumb; examiners care that the student rolls out early to north and late to south and then corrects.

The books use the words lead and lag differently. PHAK 8-26 and IFH 5-13 call the northerly turning error a 'lead' of the card and the southerly one a 'lag' [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]] [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. PHAK 8-27 and IFH 7-22 (Figure 7-35) say the compass lags on turns to or from north and leads on turns to or from south [[1:229|PHAK 8-27]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. All of them give the same action: stop the turn before the heading when turning to north, and let the card pass the heading when turning to south. Teach the action.

The trig check of the wind triangle is not in the FAA handbooks; it is the math inside an E6B. Commercial students who can do it with a calculator catch E6B setting errors, such as a magnetic course used with a true wind.

Commercial students often fly the private 3 NM and 5 minute habits. Make them call a revised ETA at every checkpoint in training, because the commercial 3 minutes is measured against it (ACS CA.VI.A.S6).
Examiners commonly cover the heading indicator or ask for a compass turn during this task. Practice it as part of navigation, not only as an instrument maneuver [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
gaps: No source gives a method or rule of thumb (such as 1 in 60 or double the drift) for how much to change heading after drifting off course. The application in this lesson is simple trig; CFI technique fills the rest.

Cruise power settings, fuel flow, TAS, leaning procedure and deviation values for your airplane come only from its POH/AFM and its own correction card. The PHAK tables and card are samples [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]] [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].
The ACS does not say how an examiner measures the 2 NM position tolerance in flight (chart estimate, GPS cross-check). Ask your CFI how local examiners do it.
The sources give TAS only by flight computer or by the 2 percent rule of thumb, not by formula [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. Use the E6B or POH for an exact number.
None of the sources covers how to fold and handle a paper chart or tablet in a busy cockpit; that is CFI technique.

activities.title: Work the leg like an E6B
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer. E6B-size differences are accepted.

items.q: TC 052, TAS 118 knots, wind 340 at 22 (true). What groundspeed do you plan?
items.why: Wind angle 340 minus 052 = 288, which is 72 degrees from the left. Crosswind 22 x sin 72 = 20.9; headwind 22 x cos 72 = 6.8. WCA = arcsin(20.9/118) = 10.2 L. GS = 118 x cos 10.2 minus 6.8 = 116.1 minus 6.8 = 109 kt (application of the wind triangle [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]]).

items.q: TC 200, TAS 145, wind 250 at 30 (true), variation 9 E, deviation from Figure 16-12. What compass heading?
items.why: Wind 50 degrees from the right: crosswind 30 x sin 50 = 23.0; WCA = arcsin(23.0/145) = 9.1, so 9 R, TH 209 [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]. East is least: MH 209 minus 9 = 200 [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Card: 0 at 180, +2 at 210, so about +1.3 at 200 (two thirds of the way). CH about 201; a 1 degree E6B difference in the WCA is accepted [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

items.q: The next checkpoint is 46 NM away and your groundspeed is 124 knots. How many minutes to get there?

A 238 NM leg at a groundspeed of 147 knots. You planned 8,000 ft (11.5 GPH) but climb to 14,000 ft on a standard day per Figure 11-28 and keep the same groundspeed. How many gallons does the leg burn at 14,000 ft?
You planned 132 knots. Two checkpoints 18 NM apart take 8 minutes, and 72 NM remain. New time to go, in minutes?
Near 36 degrees N you turn left from east to north using only the compass. With the PHAK rule, at what compass reading do you stop the turn?
items.why: Stop a turn to north 15 plus half the latitude before the heading: 15 + 18 = 33 degrees before 360, so at 033 [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

activities.title: True or false: what the chart shows
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Shaded relief on a sectional is drawn as if the light came from the northwest.
cards.why: True. Studies show our eyes are used to that view [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p.10]].

cards.s: In crowded city areas, every tall building over 200 ft AGL is shown separately.
cards.why: False. In high-density areas only the highest obstacle is shown, with the group obstacle symbol [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].

cards.s: UC next to an obstacle means its position or elevation has not been verified.
cards.why: True. UC means under construction or reported but not verified [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].

cards.s: A wind turbine's obstruction light marks the highest point of the turbine.
cards.why: False. The light is on the hub, which can be 200 to 300 ft below the unlighted blade tips [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p.11]].

cards.s: Color tints run from light green for low ground to dark brown for high ground.
The underlined name next to a VFR checkpoint flag is the checkpoint's proper name.
cards.why: True. The underline shows the proper name of the VFR checkpoint [[2:33|Chart Users' Guide p.33]].

cards.s: Basic contour lines on a sectional are spaced every 1,000 ft.
cards.why: False. Basic contours are every 500 ft, with intermediate contours often every 250 ft [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p.10]].

activities.title: Commercial checkride leg, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are on the first leg of your commercial checkride in a four-seat single, at 7,500 ft, 65 percent power, compass heading 066 planned. The examiner has covered the GPS.

steps.s: Over checkpoint 1, a town with a railroad and highway, you are 2 minutes early and about 1 NM left of the line.
options: Turn right 30 degrees now to get back on the line quickly and hold it
Keep the planned ETAs; early is fine because the plan was right
Note the time, work out the actual groundspeed and revise the ETAs
Uncover the GPS to check
steps.why: Note headings and times and adjust heading, GS and time as you go [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]]. The 3 minute standard is against the initial or revised ETA (ACS CA.VI.A.S6). One NM left is inside 2 NM, so a small heading change is enough (ACS CA.VI.A.S5).

steps.s: Checkpoint 2 should be a town with a railroad on its east side. Three minutes before its ETA you see a town ahead, but no railroad.
options: Descend 1,000 ft for a better look
Accept it and revise all the ETAs from it
Turn toward the town to read its water tower
Do not accept it yet: hold the heading and look for the railroad or the next checkpoint
steps.why: Choose checkpoints that other features confirm, and never place complete reliance on a single checkpoint. If confused, hold the heading; a turn away from it makes it easy to get lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

steps.s: While you look at the chart, the examiner points at an airplane at your 2 o'clock, same altitude, not moving in the windshield.
options: Climb 100 ft and continue
Hold course: you have the right-of-way over the airplane on your right
Give way: it is on your right and on a collision course
Wait to see if it changes course before you decide to maneuver
steps.why: When converging, the aircraft on the other's right has the right-of-way [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. A target that appears motionless is likely on a collision course [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]]. Give way and pass well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

steps.s: Back on course, you see 13 GPH on the fuel flow gauge. You planned 11.5 at this power and forgot to lean after the climb.
options: Lean per the POH and refigure fuel remaining and reserve
Add power to arrive sooner and make up for the extra fuel burn
Ignore it; the leg is short and the reserve is large enough
Switch tanks to balance the burn and keep the same mixture
steps.why: A rich mixture at altitude wastes fuel and can foul plugs; lean per the POH [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. Then compare fuel used with planned [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

steps.s: The examiner asks for your destination estimate. 52 NM remain and your last two checkpoints gave a groundspeed of 140 knots.
options: About 19 minutes, using the planned 164 knots
About 22 minutes from now
About 26 minutes
About 37 minutes
steps.why: 52 / 140 = 0.371 h = 22.3 minutes [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. Use the actual groundspeed, not the plan (ACS CA.VI.A.S6).
